rv.q: "Adolescent Salvation" builds its dramatic action slowly and cautiously, pulling you into the world of its central character, Bailey's Natasha.
It is funny, uncomfortable, heartbreaking, and ultimately a story about finding people who will stand beside you when everything changes.
Venable and Cienfuegos have found the sweet spot of capturing the full Gen Z aesthetic without falling into the trap of cringy generalizations or the overuse of internet slang.
"Adolescent Salvation" is a finely tuned, furious attack on adults too self-involved to protect their children while also meditating on the thwarted ambitions of those same adults.
This Chicago premiere, by brilliant playwright Tim Venable, speaks with a contemporary voice and picks at the facade around a teenager’s innocence, need and vulnerability.
This is a sharply observed, disturbing, morally ambiguous play that also happens to be absolutely hilarious.
"Adolescent Salvation" has engineered moments that will make you cackle and cringe, often at the same time.
It's troubling and sometimes hard to watch.

Despite the intense, adroit performances director Guillermo Cienfuegos gets from his ensemble, the play’s top notes of sardonic insight, biting humor, and gasp-inducing drama can’t conceal a vile aftertaste.

cn.t: Critics praise the sharp performances and darkly comic dialogue in this teen drama, though many take issue with its controversial attempt to humanize a pedophile. The production swings effectively from humor to tragedy.
